standard.title: Justify geographical conclusions
standard.description: evaluate data and information to justify conclusions
standard.prior_knowledge: At Y9, students evaluated data to justify conclusions (AC9HG9S04). At Y10 the same descriptor is applied with the expectation that conclusions integrate at least two geographical concepts as organisers and that justification examines whether the reasons given are adequate for the conclusion.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students draw conclusions using at least two geographical concepts as organisers and examine whether and how the reasons given justify the conclusion reached, across sustainability and wellbeing contexts.

nodes.label: Conclusions grounded in geographical concepts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can draw conclusions using at least two geographical concepts (place, space, environment, interconnection, sustainability, scale, change) as organisers for their reasoning.
nodes.minimum_width: Draw a conclusion about one geographical phenomenon using at least two named geographical concepts as organising ideas.
nodes.typical_width: Draw conclusions using at least two geographical concepts as organisers; explain how each concept contributes to the conclusion's reasoning — not just listed as labels but functioning as analytical lenses that shape what the data means.
wider: Compare conclusions drawn when using different concept pairings for the same data — evaluating how the choice of concepts shapes the analytical direction
Develop a framework for selecting which concepts are most appropriate for a given inquiry and explain the analytical justification for the selection
Examine how professional geographical conclusions in reports, articles or policy documents deploy concepts as organisers, comparing professional and student-level conclusion structures
nodes.hinge_reason: Using concepts as genuine organisers rather than decorative labels is the distinguishing feature of disciplinary geographical argument. If students simply name concepts without using them analytically, their conclusions are not geographically reasoned — and justification (Node 2) has nothing substantive to build on.

response_modes.reason: Students often append concept names to conclusions without integrating them ('this shows interconnection because things are connected'). Scaffold concept-as-organiser thinking: the concept should shape what you look at, what counts as evidence, and what the conclusion claims — not just label a pre-formed conclusion.

success_criteria: Students draw a conclusion about a geographical phenomenon and identify at least two concepts that organised their reasoning
Students explain how each concept shaped what they looked for in the data, not just what label applies

nodes.label: Evaluating the justification for a conclusion
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the reasons given for a specific decision or conclusion and explain how these reasons have or have not justified the conclusion.
nodes.minimum_width: Examine one conclusion or decision and evaluate whether the reasons given adequately justify it, identifying at least one strength and one weakness in the justification.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the reasoning behind decisions related to sustainability management or wellbeing improvement; evaluate whether the reasons given are sufficient, appropriate and internally consistent; identify where interconnected factors (environmental, economic, social, political, technological) are accounted for or overlooked.
wider: Evaluate a geographical decision from a policy document or case study — tracing the explicit and implicit reasoning, identifying assumptions, and assessing whether the conclusion follows from the evidence and arguments given
Construct an alternative conclusion from the same data and evidence, explaining what different reasoning steps would be required to reach it
Investigate a case where a decision was made and later revised — examining what new evidence or reasoning caused the revision and what that reveals about the original justification

response_modes.reason: Practising justification evaluation across both sustainability and wellbeing contexts builds the transferability of the critical reasoning skill — students who have only evaluated one type of conclusion may not apply the skill to a new context.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Justification evaluation is a portable critical reasoning skill — practising it across multiple decision types (environmental management decisions, wellbeing program decisions, policy conclusions) builds a more robust evaluative framework.
success_criteria: Students evaluate whether reasons given for a conclusion are adequate, identifying at least one strength and one gap or weakness
Students explain how interconnected factors (at least two types) were or were not accounted for in the justification
